documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: 1. Trisaccharide X
problems.statement:
Compound X is a trisaccharide which occurs principally in cottonseed meal. It does not react with Benedict's or Fehling's solutions and does not mutarotate. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis gives three different D-hexoses A,B,C. A,B and compound1 below all give the same osazone with excess acidic phenylhydrazine. C reacts with nitric acid to give optically inactive D. The Kiliani–Fischer approach establishes the configurational relation between D-glyceraldehyde and C. The intermediate aldotetrose leading to C does not give a meso compound upon nitric-acid oxidation. A with nitric acid gives optically active dicarboxylic(aldaric) acid.

Both A and B react with5mol $\mathrm{HIO_4}$.1mol A gives5mol methanoic(formic) acid and1mol methanal(formaldehyde);1mol B gives3mol formic acid,2mol formaldehyde and1mol carbon dioxide. A and B relate to the same aldotetrose, the diastereoisomer of the one related to C. Methylating X then hydrolyzing gives2,3,4-tri-O-methyl-D-hexose E from A,1,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-hexose F from B and2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-hexose G from C.

![](p1-fig1)

parts.statement: On the answer sheet draw Fischer projections of A,B,C,D.
Complete the appropriate answer-sheet Haworth projections, clearly showing E,F,G ring size and absolute stereochemistry. Either anomer is acceptable.
Underline the correct connectivity sequence of the three monosaccharides in X on the answer sheet.

sections.statement:
X does not react with Benedict's solution and does not mutarotate: it is non-reducing, so all anomeric carbons have acetal/ketal linkages. A and B give the same osazone, so have identical C3,C4,C5(and C6) stereochemistry. They differ from compound1(D-mannose) but give its osazone. One must be its C2 epimer(D-glucose), the other its C2 ketosugar(D-fructose), a deduction confirmed by later oxidative cleavage.

C gives optically inactive aldaric D on nitric-acid oxidation. Two possible aldaric acids are:

![](p1-sol-fig1)

C's precursor aldotetrose, hence D's, does not give a meso compound with nitric acid; it must be D-threose:

![](p1-sol-fig2)

Thus D is AA1 and C is D-galactose. The key prints that A reacts with5mol HI, yielding5mol formic acid and1mol formaldehyde, suggesting an aldohexose. It prints that B reacts with5mol HI, yielding4mol formic acid,1mol formaldehyde and1mol carbon dioxide, suggesting a ketohexose.

A,B relate to a tetrose different from C's, i.e.D-erythrose. Their tetrose and the resulting A=D-glucose,B=D-fructose,C=D-galactose structures are:

![](p1-sol-fig3)

Methylation followed by hydrolysis yields E,F,G below.

Only hydroxyls not involved in intra- or intermolecular acetal/ketal formation become etherified during methylation. Only E has two free hydroxyls for linking other carbohydrates, so A is central. The sequence is C–A–B(or B–A–C).

If A5 denotes A's furanose(5-membered ring),A6 its pyranose(6-membered ring),B5 B's furanose,etc., then X is C6–A6–B5. One of the4possible structure variants is:

![](p1-sol-fig7)

Note: The nature of the anomeric linkages was not specified. A's linkage to B and C may be reversed, i.e.a1,1′linkage between C and A and a1,6linkage between A and B.

problems.title: 2. Atmospheric sulfuric-acid formation
problems.statement:
Professor Molina of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology won the1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for atmospheric chemistry. One reaction studied in detail is atmospheric acid-rain formation of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. Two possible stoichiometric reactions are proposed:

Proposal A:$\mathrm{H_2O(g)+SO_3(g)\longrightarrow H_2SO_4(g)}$.

Proposal B:$\mathrm{2H_2O(g)+SO_3(g)\longrightarrow H_2SO_4(g)+H_2O(g)}$.

parts.statement:
Using simple collision theory, what reaction orders are expected for A and B?

B is thought to proceed by:

$$\mathrm{SO_3+2H_2O}\underset{k_{-1}}{\stackrel{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}}\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}\qquad\text{(fast)},$$

$$\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}\xrightarrow{k_2}\mathrm{H_2SO_4+H_2O}\qquad\text{(slow)}.$$

The complex $\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}$ is hydrogen-bond stabilized, and $k_2\ll k_1$ or $k_{-1}$.
Apply stationary(steady) states to derive the appropriate rate law and reaction order for the two-step B mechanism.

Quantum-chemical calculations give overall activation energies $E_A=+80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $E_B=-20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. State the Arrhenius relation for each and predict temperature dependence of each rate constant.
$\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ forms faster in the upper atmosphere($T=175$K) than at the surface($T=300$K). Which pathway dominates above, given part(iii)'s activation energies and Arrhenius behaviour?

sections.statement:
A:$d[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]/dt=k[\mathrm{H_2O}][\mathrm{SO_3}]$. Exponents sum to second order.

B:$d[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]/dt=k[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2$. Exponents sum to third order.

The rate law resembles an enzymatic process with rapid reversible binding followed by slow reaction. Steady state gives:

$$\frac{d[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]}{dt}=k_1[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2-k_{-1}[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]-k_2[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]=0.$$

Thus

$$k_{-1}[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]+k_2[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]=k_1[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2,$$

$$[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]=\frac{k_1[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2}{k_{-1}+k_2}.$$

Also $d[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]/dt=k_2[\mathrm{SO_3\cdot2H_2O}]$. Substitution gives

$$\frac{d[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]}{dt}=\frac{k_1k_2[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2}{k_{-1}+k_2}.$$

Since $k_2\ll k_{-1}$ this reduces to

$$\frac{d[\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]}{dt}=\frac{k_1k_2[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2}{k_{-1}}=K_{\mathrm{eq}}k_2[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2=k[\mathrm{SO_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]^2,$$

also third order.

Arrhenius:$k=Ae^{-E/RT}$.

A:$k=Ae^{-E_A/RT}=Ae^{-83.6/RT}$, increasing with $T$.

For B only the slow step is critical to temperature dependence. The very stable complexation step explains negative activation energy. B:$k=Ae^{-E_B/RT}=Ae^{+83.60/RT}$, decreasing with $T$.

Assuming comparable pre-exponential factors as usual, the reaction is faster at upper-atmosphere lower temperatures, so B operates. The source states that the rationale for B involving relative rate-constant sizes “is nonsense and was included to balance the choices”. The rationale for A involving collision probabilities appears plausible but is not a factor: the massive negative activation energy controls the situation.
